slices.basis: Every leaf heading the selected U.S. edition's General Index (printed pp. 5*-8*) lists under the Proper of Time, the Order of Mass with a single minister, the Appendix to the Order of Mass, the Commons, Ritual Masses, Masses and Prayers for Various Needs and Occasions, Votive Masses, Masses for the Dead, and the Appendices with Preparation and Thanksgiving: 210 headings, each image-checked. A parent heading counts only through its children when it has no page of its own or shares its first child's page (the dedication anniversary, the Scrutinies); needs categories 7 and 13 have their own pages and count beside their anniversary children. Kinds are the nearest permitted kind for a heading, not a granularity claim: 20 of the 41 temporal 'celebration' headings group a Sunday with its week, a run of weekdays or a whole season. Ritual, needs, votive and dead Mass headings are recorded as 'form', the kind the 2002 body slices give those sections, although one may hold several forms, a prayer set or a Collect only. Front-matter documents, the main Order of Mass section, the Proper of Saints month headings and the two further indexes are outside these targets and stated as boundaries. U.S. recension only: these headings do not duplicate, replace or reconcile the 184 PC-S composition keys of postconciliar-temporal-composition-registry, and they assert no correspondence to the Latin 2002/2008 slices, including the 33 Latin Common index headings. No held-row join is asserted.

A LITERARY TRANSLATION, CHOSEN AS A VOICE. Caswall, Neale, Aylward and Bute
differ materially over these five texts. The active overlay records the
maintainer's choice of Caswall as the through-line across the relevant texts;
it does not argue that Caswall is right.

The English is metrical verse and is not a clause-for-clause rendering. Where the
Latin sets a short strophe Caswall may fold two into one six-line stanza, and the
stanza divisions in the text recorded here are his and not the Missal's. He
renders no Amen and no Alleluia anywhere: every one of these five propers ends in
the Latin with an acclamation that the English simply does not have.
